title: Why Pi, omp and Hermes exist
act: Act II — Where the field is
takeaway: Four projects emphasize different values; they are not rungs on one ladder.

scenes.title: Different centers of gravity
scenes.visual: 5.1.1: diagram arranges four equal cards around an empty center, never stairs. 5.1.2: add philosophy labels marked editorial synthesis. 5.1.3: gradeBadge C and shared license strip retain the software/service distinction.

sentences.text: Pi, omp, Hermes Agent, and OpenClaw emphasize different design priorities, rather than forming a sequence of upgrades.
Pi centers on control; omp integrates developer tools; Hermes emphasizes persistent learning; OpenClaw connects a personal assistant to devices and chats.
All four publish MIT-licensed core repositories, while connected models, hosted services, and subscriptions keep their own terms.

onScreen.text: Editorial synthesis, not scores: Pi — control; omp — integrated developer tools; Hermes Agent — persistent learning; OpenClaw — assistant connectivity.
As of 2026-10-08 · MIT core repositories; connected services and models have separate terms.

scenes.title: Pi: control, then evolution
scenes.visual: 5.2.1: quoteCard introduces creator and date. 5.2.2–5.2.3: diagram shows original four-tool recipe beside statCard with historical conditions. 5.2.4: timeline flips to dated MCP release, keeping both dates visible. 5.2.5: diagram reveals default codemode discovery, with server tools outside direct model declarations; persistent label carries the current date and evidence chip.

sentences.text: Mario Zechner’s November 2025 account describes building Pi for predictable behavior and direct visibility into what the model sees.
sentences.spoken: Mario Zechner’s November twenty twenty-five account describes building Pi for predictable behavior and direct visibility into what the model sees.

sentences.text: His original recipe used four default tools: read, write, edit, and bash.
He reported the original system prompt and tool definitions together at below one thousand tokens.
On September twenty-ninth, twenty twenty-six, Pi added MCP, tool search, and JavaScript codemode as built-in extensions.
Its current MCP design controls which tools enter context, rather than exposing every server tool directly to the model.

onScreen.text: “if I don't need it, it won't be built” — Mario Zechner, 2025-11-30 creator account.
November 2025 original Pi recipe, creator-reported: 4 default tools (read, write, edit, bash); system prompt + tool definitions < 1,000 tokens. Not today’s configurable installation.

2026-09-29 · Pi v0.99.0 adds MCP, tool search and JavaScript codemode as built-in extensions. As of 2026-10-08, default codemode exposure discovers server tools programmatically instead of declaring each directly to the model.

scenes.title: omp: the interface matters
scenes.visual: 5.3.1–5.3.2: timeline draws one lineage arrow labelled explicit fork and repository creation, not first release. 5.3.3: diagram connects editor, language server, debugger, memory and worker nodes. 5.3.4–5.3.5: quoteCard states attributed interface thesis beside experiment caveat; no benchmark trophy.

sentences.text: omp explicitly forks Pi, with Can Bölük leading the project and Stencil Labs credited as its builder.
GitHub records the repository’s creation on December thirty-first, twenty twenty-five, a source-history milestone rather than a package-release date.
The documented integration brings together language servers, a debugger, hash-anchored edits, memory, and first-class subagents.
Bölük’s argument is that a model can understand a task yet struggle with the interface used to express its changes.
His creator-run editing experiment tested that idea by changing the edit interface while leaving the model weights alone.

onScreen.text: Pi → omp: explicit fork · repository created 2025-12-31; not a first-release claim. Led by Can Bölük; built by Stencil Labs.
As of 2026-10-08 · Documented integrated surface: LSP · DAP debugger · hash-anchored edits · memory · subagents. Integration choices, not exclusive capabilities.
“Often the model isn't flaky at understanding the task. It's flaky at expressing itself.” — Can Bölük, 2026-02-12. Creator thesis, not universal benchmark proof.

scenes.title: Hermes Agent: persistent knowledge
scenes.visual: 5.4.1: timeline introduces official release. 5.4.2: quoteCard joins memory/skill diagram; distinguish persisted files from model weights. 5.4.3: bounded store and session boundary appear. 5.4.4: split application and model-family cards with no lineage arrow between weights and learning loop.

sentences.text: Nous Research released Hermes Agent on February twenty-fifth, twenty twenty-six, aiming to carry useful knowledge across interactions.
It retains facts and reusable skills across terminal and messaging sessions, updating external state rather than training the model.
Memory depends on actual tool writes, and its bounded prompt snapshot refreshes only when a new session starts.
Hermes Agent is application software with multiple model providers, distinct from Nous Research’s separately trained Hermes model family.

onScreen.text: Hermes Agent · Nous Research official release: 2026-02-25.
“The agent that grows with you” — Nous Research, repository tagline, accessed 2026-10-08. Product aim, not measured guaranteed improvement.
As of 2026-10-08 · Memory/skills persist external state; bounded stores, actual tool writes, prompt snapshot at new session. Agent software ≠ Hermes model weights.

scenes.title: OpenClaw: connectivity and ownership
scenes.visual: 5.5.1: diagram connects personal devices and chat channels. 5.5.2: lineage map displays historical Pi integration. 5.5.3: dated current frame changes runtime ownership while retaining a Pi-TUI dependency line. 5.5.4: return to four equal philosophy cards, no ranking.

sentences.text: Peter Steinberger’s OpenClaw connects the story to assistants on personal devices and in chat channels.
Its earlier assistant integrated Pi, connecting that minimal coding toolkit to a broader personal-assistant workflow.
By October 2026, OpenClaw documents its own agent runtime, while Pi’s terminal UI toolkit remains a dependency.
sentences.spoken: By October twenty twenty-six, OpenClaw documents its own agent runtime, while Pi’s terminal UI toolkit remains a dependency.

sentences.text: Shared ancestry does not make these projects interchangeable: choose the priorities and integration boundaries that fit your work.

onScreen.text: As of 2026-10-08 · OpenClaw: personal devices, chats, user-held state and configurable providers.
Historical: Pi integration. As of 2026-10-08: OpenClaw-owned runtime; @earendil-works/pi-tui retained. Exact runtime-internalization date not established.
Four priorities, not a ladder: control · integrated tooling · persistent learning · connectivity.
